body:
## Purpose

This PR rewrites `column_reduce!`, `column_accumulate!`, and the `MatrixFields` band matrix solvers in terms of `DataLayouts.foreach_column`, so every operation that loops over columns has a unified CPU/GPU implementation and can be fused with similar operations. On GPUs, the threads assigned to each column share its work.

## Disclosure

This PR and its description were mostly generated using Claude.

## Content

- `column_reduce!`, `column_accumulate!`, and `single_field_solve!` loop over columns with `foreach_column`, through the new `DataLayouts.fold_points` and `DataLayouts.scan_points`. The CUDA kernels for integrals and for single and multiple field solves, `DataLayouts.column_reduce!`, and the caches of `single_field_solve!` are removed (`MatrixFields.single_field_solver_cache` returns `nothing`).
- On GPUs, associative operators (`+`, `*`, `max`, `min`, `&`, `|`) are reduced with warp shuffles and accumulated with Kogge-Stone scans, and other operators are applied in order by one thread per column (the new `serial` keyword of `DataLayouts.foreach_slice`).
- Tridiagonal systems on GPUs are solved by parallel cyclic reduction with any number of levels, and other band matrices (including pentadiagonal ones and others that `main` does not support) by Gaussian elimination, with their factors in registers or shared memory instead of cache fields.
- On GPUs, the band matrix solves of a `BlockDiagonalSolve` share one loop when their arguments fit in the parameter memory of a kernel.
- Commutative column reductions are no longer folded in order on CPUs or GPUs, so their results can change in the last bits.
- CPU reductions use `@simd` loops or interleaved accumulators that vectorize, and the threads of a CPU pool use the compiled fold of a one-thread reduction.
- GPU kernels take each array of a layout as a pointer, with only the extents that the type of the layout does not fix (`CompactDeviceArray`).
- In a GPU loop over columns, `column_reduce!` into a temporary with a single point runs on the thread that owns the point, which shares the result with the other threads of the column (on `main`, they read uninitialized registers).
- In a loop over columns, `similar(field, space)` allocates its result in the scope of `field`, so that column integrals can write into temporaries on other spaces.

## Comparison against main

Benchmarks of the operations themselves:

- On an AMD EPYC 7513 CPU (Julia 1.13.3, 63 levels, one thread), `column_integral_definite!` is about 4.2x faster, `column_accumulate!` 2.1x, `column_reduce!` with `max` 1.7x, `column_integral_indefinite!` 1.4x, `sum` of a Field 1.3x, and a tridiagonal `ldiv!` 8% faster.
- On an A100 (63 levels, Float64), `ldiv!` with a tridiagonal block takes 0.31–0.36 ms (`main`: 0.31 ms), and with a pentadiagonal block 1.65 ms (`main`: 1.72 ms).
- First calls take longer: 15–40% for CPU integrals and accumulations and 2–3x for CPU `max` and `min` reductions, and about 25% in total for GPU kernels of integrals, reductions, accumulations, and solves. Reductions on 4 CPU threads compile about 40% faster.

Each row compares this PR at `40fda1d4e` ([8367](https://buildkite.com/clima/climacore-ci/builds/8367), [162](https://buildkite.com/clima/climaland-downstream/builds/162), [799](https://buildkite.com/clima/climaatmos-downstream/builds/799), [804](https://buildkite.com/clima/climacore-end-to-end-performance/builds/804)) with `main` ([8360](https://buildkite.com/clima/climacore-ci/builds/8360), [155](https://buildkite.com/clima/climaland-downstream/builds/155), [789](https://buildkite.com/clima/climaatmos-downstream/builds/789), [796](https://buildkite.com/clima/climacore-end-to-end-performance/builds/796)), except the AMIP kernel rows, which profile both in one job ([806](https://buildkite.com/clima/climacore-end-to-end-performance/builds/806), on a temporary branch with the same source code as this PR). Build 8360 ran CliMA/ClimaCore.jl#2718, which has the same source code as `main`, and its downstream builds ran older commits of ClimaLand and ClimaAtmos than 162 and 799. Rows over several jobs or cases give the min / median / max of the PR values, the `main` values, and the per-job ratios, over those that passed in both builds on the same hardware; wall-time rows only include jobs that took at least a minute in both builds and did not precompile packages. The tables leave out the six jobs that run the data loop, mapreduce, MatrixFields solver, and column integral tests, to which this PR adds tests. The data loop tests on 4 CPU threads, for example, take 1.8 instead of 1.3 min, and their 160 new tests take 35 s.

title: Enable fusion of column reductions, accumulations, and solves

body:
## Purpose

This PR builds on #2697 by fusing `field_matrix_solve!` on GPUs: all of the operations of a `FieldMatrixSolver` run in one loop over columns, which launches one kernel per solve. On CPUs, every operation keeps its own loop over columns. On all devices, solvers skip work that the structure of the system makes redundant.

## Disclosure

This PR and its description were mostly generated using Claude.

## Content

- `field_matrix_solve!` (and `ldiv!` of a `FieldMatrixWithSolver`) runs all block operations and band matrix solves of an algorithm in one GPU kernel, unless the algorithm stores Fields or logs debug information, its Fields differ in masks or column shapes, or its arguments do not fit in the parameter memory of the kernel.
- Solvers whose band matrix solves all run on one thread per column (pentadiagonal and other band matrices that are not tridiagonal) are not fused, since the other threads of each column would wait for them.
- Solvers have no caches: `run_field_matrix_solver!(alg, x, A, b, [previous_x, pool])` evaluates right-hand sides and increments lazily, in registers or shared buffers in a fused kernel or into Fields from a pool that is allocated once otherwise.
- A `FieldNameDict` in a loop over columns is sliced like its Fields, and its key operations are computed once per type by `@generated` helpers, which shortens the inference of fused kernels.
- Solvers evaluate the entries that they combine at literal indices, so that GPU inference never joins lazy entries of different types, and functions that a fused kernel calls are inlined explicitly, so that Julia 1.12 and later leave no register arrays on the stack or heap.
- Fused kernels are compiled with at most 80 registers per thread, every statement reads its thread index with an opaque instruction, and the iterations of a `StationaryIterativeSolve` are compiled without loop-invariant code motion (`Utilities.@disable_licm`), so that addresses are not kept in registers.
- In a fused kernel, lazy stencil entries over the same columns are evaluated in one loop over points, the rows of each parallel cyclic reduction are loaded before the solve that precedes it, and the solution stays in shared memory when it fits.
- `StationaryIterativeSolve` starts from `x[1] = inv(P) * b` when `x[0]` is zero, and solvers skip the solves of right-hand sides that are zero by structure, which only changes the signs of zeros.
- `StationaryIterativeSolve` without a preconditioner or with a diagonal one computes every increment of `x` before updating `x`. On `main`, the update reads `x` at neighboring levels while writing it, a data race on GPUs that converges faster than the documented iteration, so solves can need more iterations.

## Comparison against #2697

Each row compares this PR at `cf36369a2` ([8368](https://buildkite.com/clima/climacore-ci/builds/8368), [163](https://buildkite.com/clima/climaland-downstream/builds/163), [798](https://buildkite.com/clima/climaatmos-downstream/builds/798), [805](https://buildkite.com/clima/climacore-end-to-end-performance/builds/805)) with #2697 at `40fda1d4e` ([8367](https://buildkite.com/clima/climacore-ci/builds/8367), [162](https://buildkite.com/clima/climaland-downstream/builds/162), [799](https://buildkite.com/clima/climaatmos-downstream/builds/799), [804](https://buildkite.com/clima/climacore-end-to-end-performance/builds/804)). Rows over several jobs or cases give the min / median / max of the PR values, the #2697 values, and the per-job ratios, over those that passed in both builds on the same hardware; wall-time rows only include jobs that took at least a minute in both builds and did not precompile packages. The tables leave out the MatrixFields GPU unit tests, to which this PR adds 34 solver tests. They take 16.2 instead of 12.1 min, and the solver test takes 8.0 instead of 4.6 min. The first AMIP coupling step, which compiles the fused solver, takes 245 s instead of 222 s and allocates 56.3 GiB instead of 50.8 GiB ([805](https://buildkite.com/clima/climacore-end-to-end-performance/builds/805) and [804](https://buildkite.com/clima/climacore-end-to-end-performance/builds/804)).

## Profiling results

Each row compares the profiling jobs of this PR at `cf36369a2` and of `main` (without #2697) in [807](https://buildkite.com/clima/climacore-end-to-end-performance/builds/807), which profile 10 calls of `field_matrix_solve!` in the flagship AMIP configuration and the ClimaLand models on an A100, with Nsight Compute on one call. `PR (unfused)` profiles this PR with fusion turned off, and its register and occupancy values, like those of `main`, give the min / median / max over the kernels of a call. The fused AMIP kernel is limited to 12 blocks of 64 threads per multiprocessor by both registers and shared memory, and stalls mostly on global memory latency, without spills. DRAM writes vary between profiles of the same kernels, because only part of the data that a kernel writes leaves the L2 cache before the kernel ends: `main`'s snowy land solve wrote 28.6 MB here and 7.96 MB in [795](https://buildkite.com/clima/climacore-end-to-end-performance/builds/795), with the same 85.8 MB of reads.
